nice.say: Nice used to be an insult.

nice.show: 700 years ago, calling someone *nice* meant you thought they were a *fool.*
nice.say: Seven-hundred years ago, calling someone nice meant you thought they were a fool.

nice.show: It comes from the Latin *nescius,* meaning *ignorant.*
nice.say: It comes from the Latin NESS-ee-us, meaning ignorant.

nice.show: It travelled through *Old French* into English around the 1300s.
nice.say: It travelled through Old French into English around the thirteen-hundreds.
Then it drifted. Fussy, then shy, then precise.

nice.show: Until, in the 1700s, it finally meant *pleasant.*
nice.say: Until, in the seventeen-hundreds, it finally meant pleasant.

nice.show: So when someone calls you *nice,* it took 700 years to become a *compliment.*
nice.say: So when someone calls you nice, it took seven-hundred years to become a compliment.

silly.say: Silly used to be a compliment.
In Old English, SAY-lee meant blessed, happy, lucky.

silly.show: Its cousin is still alive in German: *selig,* still meaning *blessed.*
silly.say: Its cousin is still alive in German. ZAY-lish, still meaning blessed.
Over centuries the spelling shifted. SAY-lee, SEE-lee, silly.

silly.show: and the meaning slid: *innocent,* then *pitiable,* then *foolish.*
silly.say: And the meaning slid. Innocent, then pitiable, then foolish.
From blessed to foolish. Language is wild.

muscle.show: Every time you flex, you're showing off a *little mouse.*
muscle.say: Every time you flex, you're showing off a little mouse.
Muscle comes from Latin MUSS-coo-luss, meaning little mouse.

muscle.show: The Romans thought a flexing muscle looked like a *mouse* moving under the skin.
muscle.say: The Romans thought a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin.

muscle.show: And the same word gave us another animal: the *mussel.*
muscle.say: And the same word gave us another animal. The mussel.
So your biceps are, technically, mice.

goodbye.say: Goodbye is a prayer in disguise.

goodbye.show: In the 1500s, people said *God be with ye.*
goodbye.say: In the fifteen-hundreds, people said God be with ye.

goodbye.show: Said fast, again and again, it got squashed: *godbwye.*
goodbye.say: Said fast, again and again, it got squashed. God-bwye.

goodbye.show: Then *good day* and *good night* rubbed off on it, and *God* became *good.*
goodbye.say: Then good day and good night rubbed off on it, and God became good.

goodbye.show: Its neighbours do the same: *adieu* and *adiós* both mean *to God.*
goodbye.say: Its neighbours do the same. Ah-DYUH and ah-DYOSE both mean to God.
So every goodbye is a tiny blessing.

ampersand.show: The alphabet used to have *27 letters.*
ampersand.say: The alphabet used to have twenty-seven letters.

ampersand.show: And you still use the last one every day.
ampersand.say: And you still use the last one every day.

ampersand.show: Two thousand years ago, Romans wrote *et,* Latin for *and.*
ampersand.say: Two thousand years ago, Romans wrote ett, Latin for and.

ampersand.show: Written fast, over and over, the *E* and *t* fused into one *symbol.*
ampersand.say: Written fast, over and over, the E and T fused into one symbol.

ampersand.show: In the 1800s, kids recited it right after *Z,* as a letter.
ampersand.say: In the eighteen-hundreds, kids recited it right after zee, as a letter.

ampersand.show: Saying *and* alone sounded odd, so they said *and per se and,* meaning 'and, by itself'.
ampersand.say: Saying and alone sounded odd, so they said, and per say and, meaning, and, by itself.

ampersand.show: Mumbled fast, it blurred into one word…
ampersand.say: Mumbled fast, it blurred into one word.

ampersand.show: Some fonts still show the *E* and *t* hiding inside.
ampersand.say: Some fonts still show the E and T hiding inside.

ampersand.show: So every *&* you write is a *2,000-year-old* Latin word.
ampersand.say: So every ampersand you write is a two-thousand-year-old Latin word.

amp2.show: The alphabet didn't always end at *Z.*
amp2.say: The alphabet didn't always end at zee.

amp2.show: 200 years ago, kids finished it with one more: X, Y, Z… *and.*
amp2.say: Two-hundred years ago, kids finished it with one more. Ex, why, zee, and.
Well, not the word. The symbol.
And it was hiding a secret.

amp2.show: Ancient Roman scribes wrote *et,* Latin for 'and', so often…
amp2.say: Ancient Roman scribes wrote ett, Latin for and, so often,

amp2.show: that the *E* and the *t* began to *melt* together.
amp2.say: that the E and the T began to melt together.

amp2.show: Until they became one shape. *This* one.
amp2.say: Until they became one shape. This one.

amp2.show: So kids ended the alphabet chanting *and per se and:*
amp2.say: So kids ended the alphabet chanting, and per say and.

amp2.show: A name born from a *classroom chant.*
amp2.say: A name born from a classroom chant.

amp2.show: Some fonts still show the *E* and the *t.*
amp2.say: Some fonts still show the E and the T.

amp2.show: So next time you type it, remember: you're writing *Latin.*
amp2.say: So next time you type it, remember. You're writing Latin.
